25:Running a new language model on every benchmark is costly, yet leaderboards hold many earlier scores. We ask which $k$ benchmarks to run on a new model so that its remaining scores can be inferred, and how large $k$ must be. We study factor-model prediction with greedy Bayesian A-optimal selection (it chooses benchmarks one at a time to minimise the average posterior variance of the unrun scores) under a protocol that holds out whole model families and uses paired, family-clustered intervals, on dense blocks of MTEB embedding-model results and the 57 subjects of HELM MMLU, and on MTEB matrices with missing cells; we do not test suites of benchmarks for generative language models. Three benchmarks close 81--96\% of the gap between the column-mean predictor and a leave-one-benchmark-out predictor, but 90\% needs one benchmark on HELM MMLU and nine or more on MTEB, with wide intervals. shown.message:
I approved `paper-repo`#9 at head `78d468d`. The merge still waits on `figtab-repo` and `venue-repo`.

Both changes I required are in:
- **Scope:** the abstract and the introduction now name the data (MTEB embedding results and the 57 subjects of HELM MMLU). They say the paper does not test benchmark suites for generative language models, where our dense blocks have N<12.
- **Novelty claim:** it now reads "Among the work we read, none ...".

The abstract also now describes the selector as choosing benchmarks one at a time. I did not look at whether the other optional items (a cited source for the pivoted-QR and leverage-score baselines, a clause on adaptive testing) were picked up.

I read the new Section 6.3 and discussion wording, and it matches the pre-registered H2 and H4 outcomes. It says plainly that the factor model buys no accuracy over simple predictors, and that the selector's gain is modest and shared by simpler selectors.

I have nothing else open besides commitment issue #2.
